en: Collected Table of Contents for the Poems of Mutual Response between the Two Forests by Zhiguizi.
Four Poems Spontaneously Composed by Peng Shaosheng;
Four Poems in Response by Wang Yuanliang; Four Poems on "Knowing One's Return" Spontaneously Narrated by Zhiguizi;
Four Poems in Reply to Zhuxiangzi, Universally Presented to All Fellow Students.
Luo Yougao, upon learning that Zhiguizi had composed four "Spontaneous Verses" and that Zhu Xiangzi had composed four matching verses,
rejoiced and praised them, also composing four matching verses;
Wang Jin likewise matched Zhiguizi’s four "Spontaneous Verses."
A Postscript to a Poetic Exchange between the Two Forest-Dwellers of Gaoyou, including four occasional verses by Peng Shaosheng on past events, inscribed upon a poem and letter.
He often drafted strategies for governing the world; his lofty aspirations took Gaofu and Kaixi as his teachers. Now, upon the celestial highway, he spreads his six-feathered wings.
Climbing high, I gaze down at the floating clouds; once gone, they leave no trace. A long song enters the thatched hut; from dream I awaken to the whiteness of the eastern window.

Abiding in the state of Qi, I knock upon the primordial gate; I practice the refinement of qi, longing for rejuvenation. I await the cinnabar script from the Nine Heavens; I look forward to the blue birds of the Three Isles.

The autumn wind blows through the strands of my hair; yellow leaves share its withered state. Incense is burned and I attain the state of "sitting-forgetfulness"; everything before my eyes is vast and expansive.
Pure water brings forth the lotus pedestal; radiance arises from every crevice. Turning my mind toward the Western Pond, all is suddenly illuminated as one.

The causes and conditions of saṃsāra are severed; through cultivation and practice, one attains the essential gateway. Turning my gaze back, I pity those throughout the kalpas who have long laughed at clay figurines.

Human life is bound to Jambudvīpa; great afflictions lie in delusion and attachment. Who has achieved the merit of a single victory, sitting in peaceful leisure while the weeds and reeds are naturally cleared?
In an araṇya one finds sufficient peace; it is good to partake together of the *īpika* (vegetarian offerings). Master Huiyuan recited his liturgy during the six periods of the day;
with every final drop of the bell’s toll, he dwelt in dhyāna. Harmony knows how to return to the child;

these four verses were composed by me, Wang Yuanliang, on the sentient beings of the *saṃsāra* realm: they consume evil as if it were food and drink; the karmic conditions are dark and obscure, and their delusions pervade the six directions.

Constricted and narrow; at dawn and dusk, form and breath are exhausted. Where shall the wandering soul go? Entering the cycle of rebirth from time immemorial, one falsely brings calamity and ruin upon oneself.
Crawling and fluttering, scaling like fish and winging like birds—once possessing a human countenance, now suddenly transformed.
In the four directions and above and below, all have become abodes of suffering. I sigh every time for the primordial age of the Sovereign, which abandoned me as if...

The ruins remain; the roots of my bonds to this earth have long endured. My radiant voice cannot yet reach you immediately. I contemplate it again and again; how could I sleep through the entire night?

The demon of illness gradually spies upon me, taking advantage of my moments of weakness and darkness. I look up in reliance upon the benevolence of the Creator and the power of the parents of the hidden and the manifest worlds.
Once more I encounter a generation of makers of men, who nurture me with profound grace, continuing even unto this day.

I have not yet attained immortality; alone I hold these fragmentary scrolls. In silence I feel shame for this body that has failed to repay its debts; my poverty and lowliness grow increasingly disordered.
I fear constantly that even a single thought might stray, causing me to betray the purity of this dwelling. (1)
From antiquity to the present, all that exists is transient; there is nothing that does not perish. The young grow day by day into maturity, while the mature grow day by day old.

Failing to encounter a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one falsely deems others to be clever and artful. Having heard the words of the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*), I have been able to understand through the analogy of the ocean.
Because they benefit all beings, they do not contend. They produce inexhaustible treasures; their moisture nourishes the soil like rich loam.

Vast and expansive as the azure sky, the ten thousand rivers flow toward the east. The ocean of learning laughs at the small pond. How does one study the sages? One gazes upon the sea while sitting on an island within it.

Furthermore, one contemplates hundreds of thousands of oceans. Each ocean is a path for placing the feet; each ocean is a world-system. These world-systems revolve and fold back upon themselves, dissolving and returning into the midst of their own original nature.
How then could one discuss large or small? The waters of the sea become a field of mulberry trees; that which was moist becomes parched in time.
The Dharma-stream of the Tathāgata has been vast and surging thus from time immemorial; looking back at those of the Two Vehicles, how many are like fallen leaves swept away?
To the west is Amitābha, with his eighty-four thousand excellent marks. (2)
Arising from faith, suffering is not solid; hearing the Dharma, suffering is not essential. How distant is the land? The lamp of the mind shines upon itself.
In the space of a single thought-moment, one is reborn there; a great dream suddenly becomes a great awakening. Forever free from falling back, one constantly practices the Buddha’s teachings.
That Buddha of Immeasurable Life possesses a radiance that shines afar, and his spiritual resonance calls forth these sentient beings of evil karma.
Rescue is achieved with extreme swiftness; through compassionate vows, one is skillfully guided. Women, those with physical impairments, and the weak—everyone may reach that state.
Do not harbor further doubts; simply and single-mindedly hold the name of Amitābha. You shall arrive in that Land of Ultimate Bliss and enjoy sublime purity for ten thousand kalpas.

The birds cry out the emptiness of impermanence; their melodic calls are resonant yet not clamorous (the vulgar term being *zào*). The wind in the forest is the sound of celestial music, winding and turning as it arises from the deep hollows.
A single pool of merit-water is encircled by jeweled railings; yellow, green, and white flowers stand tall, emerging from the mud.
Within, they sever the afflictions of the three poisons; without, they dismiss the clamor of the various māras. The Bodhisattvas act as virtuous friends, leading one far away from all [defilements].
Arrogant. Having already attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), his power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) cannot be disturbed.

Returning to the triple world (*traidhātuka*), he shatters the darkness like the sun’s radiance. Turning back toward Jambudvīpa, he assumes the appearance of a humble servant. At that time, upon seeing the World-Honored One, he would rather incur the World-Honored One’s reproach.
If this meaning is not false, I shall diligently proclaim it for the sake of the ignorant; if this meaning is otherwise, I shall long remain as one of wisdom.
He laughed (3). Recalling the past, when I was six or seven years old, I had a profound aspiration for the written word; I feared only that I might not conform to the Dharma.
Weeping, I felt a sense of lingering attachment. Now, at thirty-three, the years have passed in silence. From moment to moment (*kṣaṇa-tatkṣaṇa*), I reflect with subtle mindfulness.

As for these transformations: though the hair on the crown has already turned blue and white, the face is not yet wrinkled; the essential nature does not shift for a moment, and the sun and moon do not long remain in *dhyāna*.

This originally wondrous, perfect luminosity causes the faculty of faith to manifest accordingly. Though sins have persisted for immeasurable kalpas, they melt away like ice and snow to reveal what was there all along.
That one Buddha is all Buddhas—this is unimpeded eloquence (*apratihatapratibhāna*). That one land is all lands—this is knowledge.
The Perfectly Universal [Vehicle] aids all ordinary beings still bound by every fetter, like one who wishes to prepare a magnificent meal from grains as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
therefore, the practice of the Way is difficult, and many often sigh in vain admiration. Reading books and composing poems for oneself, the Dharma-gate opens up skillful means.
Knowing the home and attaining that to which one belongs—may you act as my guide first. (4)
In Response to "Zhuxiangzi" and Presented to My Fellow Students, Four Poems. By Peng Shaosheng.
I observe that in Jambudvīpa, slaughter is practiced for food and drink; the custom of eating raw fur has existed since antiquity, yet this trend grows more urgent by the day.
In deep abysses, nets and lines are spread; in dense forests, snares and spears await. Alas, what crime have they committed that, without provocation, they are suddenly beset?
How much more so for those who ply their butcher’s knives, committing slaughter day and night! They purchase the lives of others with money, devouring them to their own satisfaction.
The large are divided among them like melons; the small are left in a heap of scattered remains. Who knows that within these bowls and platters dwell a hundred vengeful spirits?
A thousand billion [lives]—heavenly grudges and hardships remain unappeased. Transforming into malevolent spirits and *yu* demons, they suddenly regain human form once more.

Sharpening their blades to strike at enemies, they have entered the cycle of *saṃsāra* from time immemorial, alternating as host and guest. Were it not for the Great Awakened King, who could shatter such delusions?
I pray you tell me, my fellow practitioners: let us augment the power of your compassionate grace, universally proclaim the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, and let its pure influence pervade all.
In the four directions, chickens and pigs roam unrestrained; fish and birds frolic together in joy. This vow is truly difficult to fulfill; how can I set aside my longing?
Knowing that you do not treat me with neglect, I shall soon behold the white lotus.
How tall and stately is the lotus, standing alone beyond the eight directions! Transplanted into the midst of the mire, its branches and tendrils painfully entwine it.

When one washes away the defilements and perceives its original root, the water becomes clear and the flower’s color bright. In the silent night it emits a wondrous light; within that light, the worlds are beautiful.

A snap of the fingers transforms east and west; the cessation of the mind equalizes the great and the small. Immortal music plays in the empty forest; the sound of the Dharma resonates through the singing birds.
My longing is now tranquil; the intent of all things is hushed and still. *Namo Amitābha*. One thing understood, all is understood.

The ocean of awakening is vast and boundless; the fundamental nature of all sentient beings is subtle and wondrous. Yet, following the current while ignorant of the true source, they do not reckon with birth and death.
Out of great compassion, the Tathāgata diligently issues this proclamation for your sake: the Confucians cultivate their constancy, and the Laozi contemplates the ultimate limit.

Since time immemorial within the triple world, there has never been two luminaries in a single month. Yet, as your manifested bodies pervade all responsive capacities, ten thousand reflections share in the same tranquil illumination.
This truth is indeed evidenced by reality; it would be mere senility for me to say otherwise. The various devas and humans of the Great Brahma Heaven all submit to the Tathāgata’s teaching.
Alas, in this age of the Final Dharma, all cling to appearances and clamor in confusion; they vainly attempt to shoot at empty space—how could they ever encompass the vast universe?

We, you and I, share a common heart; though we know the kindness [of the Buddhas], we have never repaid it. We vow to exhaust our births from the very beginning and shall always serve as guides for the world.
I leisurely wander through the gates of Nirvana; there is neither dream nor waking.

I have heard that Liu Zhong'en delighted in practicing the visualization of the Western Paradise, and there was also Pang Daoyuan, who spent his days constantly in the company of his wife and children.
Ascending together to the field of quiescent extinction, how could heart and trace ever be distinguished? Rebirth attained as non-birth—these two meanings are one and the same thread.
To this day we look up to the trailing light; its lofty banner is planted in the Milky Way. This humble youth looks back to the former masters; our natural kinship holds deep affection.

Though entering the mountains, I still linger in hesitation; I have cleared the chamber to welcome a pure retreat. Yet, what I intend to accomplish remains unfinished; I sit... (Note: The final character "坐" [zuò] indicates the sentence is left incomplete.)

As the year draws to a close, I wave my hand in farewell to the drifting clouds. Beholding this body as identical to a flash of lightning, if the ocean of desire does not dry up, how can the evil realms ever be severed?
Knowing where one must return, one must return; in coming and going, there is no lingering attachment.
Having learned that Guizi had composed a poem and that Zhuxiangzi had written a response, I was filled with joy and admiration, and thus composed four verses in response:
Lu Yougao, High Tone, opens the void of the kalpa;
Opening his eyes, he craves food and drink. He nurtures the worms of the sense-faculties; The stirring movements give rise to the karma-consciousness.

In an instant, male and female are distinguished; in a flash, lustful thoughts press in. As mental conceptions flow and intermingle within the interval of craving (the vulgar term for which is "love"), the two colors [of subject and object] meet in a circular embrace.

A single deluded thought from time immemorial causes one to sit amidst the confusions of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Through inversion, various species emerge; as they revolve, they fill the world.

The perceived portion (*darśana-bhāga*) and the perceived-as-object portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) arise, drawing boundaries across what is originally a single entity. Thus, the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and mind, together with the body, are formed.
The six states do not know one another; they act as thieves toward each other, each insatiable in their greed.

In their ignorance, they pursue only what they can grasp, while the people stand tall and rigid like trees upon two peaks. Amidst this, malice does not cease to stir; they attack and seize through arbitrary entrapment. Those of the same kind change places like heads and tails, yet how could they refrain from inflicting slaughter? Every species calls out to its own faction and herd; the strong and the weak are as [unstable as]— (Note:

The final phrase "如" (rú) indicates a comparison or simile that was likely followed by a character or phrase describing instability or lack of order, such as "如風" (like the wind) or "如雲" (like clouds), which has been omitted in the source text.)

Rolling up the mats, with deep and lingering sorrow, at first both humans and beasts lay in utter disorder. We reverently contemplate the ancient sages and saints, who manifested their transformations to establish the pinnacle of human conduct.

They clarified the relationships between kin and established the principles of righteousness, correcting the excesses of lustful desires. They utilized objects to express profound grief and diligently embodied the teachings of agriculture and reaping.

Those who were fierce and predatory were driven away to distant, secluded places; through harmonious consultation, the office of the Minister of Sacrifices was established, so that all things, high and low, became docile and compliant.

The scales [fly/strange]. Benevolent winds arrive and the majestic phoenix no longer unbinds its neck-ring by the sounding stones. At this time, the commoners of the lower realm are weary and oppressed; they find no peace in their daily toil.

Yet they continue their labors in plowing and weaving, and longevity brings them manifold blessings. Amidst these times, order and chaos intermingle; the nature of the people is exhausted by deception and change.
Evil habits layer upon layer like filth and entanglements; the light of their nature falls into deep darkness. [In the midst of it,] greed and the greed for killing roll on—

The fruit fell away. In middle antiquity, clans became distinct; suspicions arose as one sought to distinguish the minute and the profound. Before long, the dykes were breached, and disaster began with the chink of a single moth.
The music of Zheng and Wei spread like a wave; its lingering currents grew ever more perilous and severe. Quilts and pillows became fields for spears and halberds;

flesh and blood flew before whistling arrows. Thus was the foundation for the world’s ruin laid. Following the old ways step by step, they added to this the calamity of gluttony, becoming as sticky as glue.

Stuck fast, it is difficult to brush clean. In times of peace, material resources abound; for feasting guests, one slaughters life. For rites of capping, marriage, mourning, and sacrifice, who sighs at the hacking and carving?

When a person is in a state of grief or rage, they willfully cook and dismember living beings. In the midst of a person’s field of joy, the feelings of those creatures are all the more piteous and sorrowful.
Forced to endure the suffering of their brief lives, their flesh fills the rifts of the seven emotions. Once they enter the cauldron, they cry out and leap; down—

Their throats still make a rasping sound. Why do they not recall the evils of past lives? They merely record the enemies of this life. Because of drought-demons and pestilence, people are foolish and know no trepidation.
Otherwise, they become jackals and tigers; otherwise, they become *gǔ* and *yù* (poisonous insects). Some move secretly within people; some dwell in the liver and diaphragm.
The various diseases of sentient beings undergo ten thousand transformations that are difficult to fathom. They cause the living to swell and the dead to rot.

Within [this world], there are hundreds of billions of vengeful insects; their forms are described in ancient texts. They gnaw and suck like silkworms devouring silk. For what reason do you take pleasure in karmic retribution?
Because you have discharged your vital essence for them. Otherwise, one would regain a human body; instead, they howl with their kind, spreading calamities, manifesting the faces of rākṣasas.

In pits and slaughterhouses, they take joy in the accumulation of grievances. I have observed the histories of former dynasties: through lust and murder, each new era was opened up. Their extraordinary agonies are unbearable to witness.
I say: often it wounds the heart and causes deep distress. Alas! It has been long since the Sage departed; his teachings have become fragmented and divergent.

On the outside, they present the words of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius; on the inside, they expand the dwellings of form and food. With caps and robes arrayed and bells and drums sounding, they exhaust themselves in bows and prostrations according to ritual protocol.

Yet, when one examines the origins of these sprouts, the two ends remain clearly distinct. Like a sheep wearing a tiger’s fur, all falsely rely upon the walls of the Sage to echo through the entire *saha* world.
Painful! Mechanical and artificial from the past, I happened to hear the precepts against hatred and delusion; I laughed so hard that my cap fell off. Is it truly because my nature is thus?
It is the power of the forces of past karma. Like a puppet-master manipulating marionettes, one willingly accepts the service of demons and ghosts.

There are many of keen faculties who, bound by attachment, dread change; they step forward only to retreat again, their doubts and regrets constricting them on all sides, as they hide their roots in the subtle.
Vast and empty! To grasp at a speck of dust is already to be alienated; to part lips and produce frivolous arguments is but a farce, full of tangled complications.
Hearing this, one can do nothing but straighten one’s robes, sit in silence, and sigh: "Alas, I have fallen for so long, delighting in the internal and feasting on the flesh of craving.

Yet, with a single subtle movement, I strike against the highest heavens; like clear ice, I solidify the brine of delusion. Through the conditions of reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, I mistakenly treat its words as a mere seal; yet therein lies the certainty of purity.

Instruction: My correct faith has not been tempered or made straight; it has wandered aimlessly for many springs now. Daily, the various defilements have increased. Moved by the grace of the Great Compassionate One’s vow, he has gathered me in, leaving no trace of my perversities.
Yet I cast myself into a thicket of obstacles and difficulties; the precious jewel was but a fleeting glimpse upon my robe.

Although it does not appear again, if one can immediately [apply oneself], one should universally contemplate the meditation on impurity. The fire of the four great elements blazes forth; contemplate it again.
Contemplating the return to the source, the flavors of form leave no lingering trace. I vow to the end of the future, never daring to neglect my protective mindfulness.
Having attained unimpeded eloquence, I penetrate all veils and obstructions. May the twelve classes of beings forever be removed from the registers of birth and death.
Namo Amitābha. Grant me the white radiance of your brow-hair.
I contemplate the Chapter on the Great Vows: boundless and without origin, it knows how to slice through subtle atoms with a blade, yet encompasses the vast expanse of the great chiliocosm.
Within twenty-one billion lands, each and every realm is transformed and purified; the forty-eight kings of vows are each adorned with sublime beauty.

One, two, three, four, five. With these five vows, may afflictions be purified; may the three evil realms be made level with radiant light; may those in the womb and prisons be transformed into lotus cradles;

may food and clothing arrive as soon as one recites the name; may palaces and pavilions be adorned with exquisite jewels; and may various harmonious fragrances be blended, so that through every scent, the Buddha-way is practiced.
In every matter, all seeking has ceased; each and every thing is inlaid with the seven treasures. Alas for Jambudvīpa! They employ these things to indulge in craftiness and guile.

Like empty bubbles forming upon the ocean of desire, the four elements entwine one another; when they fall to the ground, one wails and weeps, realizing too late that one’s remorse was not felt sooner.

Following along with habitual tendencies toward external objects, scenes and events succeed one another in confusion. As these habits multiply, attachment arises; as they endure, greed and delusion are produced.

Having learned that the sugarcane staff is sweet, one instead pities the distress of emerging from the womb. Food, beauty, fields, houses, and clothing—these are all managed and calculated to the very limit of their subtle essence.
Mouths know only how to stop at sufficiency, yet minds constantly calculate gain and loss. Regardless of noble or base, wise or foolish, each remains unaware of aging.

Because the ground of the mind sits thus neglected and overgrown, few succeed in sweeping it clean for long. They casually bestow their surplus wealth, yet demand recompense as harshly as an executioner.
To be able to cultivate tainted karma is already to rank among the mediocre; yet, lamentably, one’s roots of virtue are deluded, like discussing hunger and satiety while eating a painted cake.
How much more so when one plunders others—how could an upward-pointing arrow not strike back? Wandering through all three miserable realms, false illusions become poisonous disturbances.

I universally pray that all sentient beings, who are uplifted by the power of fearlessness, may rejoice in those spontaneous blessings. With minds intent on mindfulness through day and night, I now perform this dedication here.
May even the slightest doubt fall away into the vast void. Homage to Amitābha, who extends his hand from beyond the blue lotus.

Blue lotuses surge forth with fragrant light; the exquisite *utpala* flowers are wondrous. The Tathāgata Twelve Lights—light upon light, blazing like radiant lotuses—their roots rest in the void, universally upholding and universally enshrouding all.
Alas! You have long since fled and departed, violating the covenant with your compassionate father.
Such a wondrous lotus pedestal—how it has been defiled, insulted, and utterly destroyed by violence! I reverently contemplate its pure form, which remains unchanged through all conditions;
it stands tall, emerging from the mud, never stained by the mire or sludge. Yet I only regret that it withers and falls, unable to remain forever in full bloom and awakening.
Lofty is Śākyamuni; from his lotus tongue he has suspended the sacred scriptures. He modeled and depicted the Honored One of Ultimate Bliss, providing guidance most clear and direct.

Yet when the transformations of sentient beings become difficult, they hear this and merely laugh it off. Instead, through simple and easy methods, their own doubts and suspicions become like a self-imposed cage.
The tree is as vast as my canopy and banner; false speech follows the chirping of cicadas. The *Avataṃsaka* and the Pure Land—both the provisional and the ultimate shine forth together.
Like Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, they are the names of the three sages of the *Avataṃsaka*. Nāgārjuna emerged from the Dragon Palace; how earnest is his vow to be reborn there!
These three great Bodhisattvas—how could they have been negligent in their decline? Furthermore, as for Śūramgama and Śrī-Ābhāsvara, they set forth their meritorious achievements;

with single-minded devotion, they were like a mother and child, cherishing one another through kalpas. Through the ripening of the pure karma of *gomayakhādan* (the cow-chewing vow), they have thus escaped the retribution of being a cow-chewer.

These, along with hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, are equally essential for perfect penetration. To speak of passing or failing the examinations is like trying to glue the bridge-pins of a lute once they have already split.

Whether it be the mind of Chan or the mind of the Pure Land, let every thought be free from agitation; let the mindfulness of the Buddha and the mindfulness of sentient beings hook one another together in every moment.

The *guoluo* wasp calls out to the *mínglíng* caterpillar; truly, through this single act of transformation, they become its likeness. A domestic hen broods over pheasant eggs, yet the emergence from the shell depends on the chick’s own pecking.

How much more so for one who gives birth to a Buddha—since we are of one essence, why feel regret or distress? The spiritual mentors of successive generations have repeatedly exhorted us to strive in generating the aspiration for enlightenment.
His words are luminous and pure; he probes the profound mysteries of the Pure Land. Worldly men, bound by deep karma, read his work and loathe its boldness.

Yet, hearing it with a clear mind, they do not harbor doubts; the banner of their inner resolve turns like a wind-swept standard. My friend, the one who knows the way home, illuminates the clamor of the swarming gnats.

Tearing open his mouth, he extends his crimson tongue, like one attempting to dam a collapsing torrent. Lofty indeed amidst the Dharma of the Final Age, his celestial bone-structure is truly heroic and formidable.
I pray that you go against the current, turning back to hear the majestic resonance within the nine apertures. *Namo Amitābha*. Free from contention, let forth a pure whistle.
My friend, you who know the way home, your longing heart has been steadfast through our long separation. You have sent me a letter, its perilous words causing my weary spirit to startle.
Within it are seven or eight verses, as fragrant and pure as lotus petals. I know your heart; you delight in goodness, and we shall together offer up that virtue.

I have again read the lines from "Bamboo Fragrance," where the vast ocean tides roll back to reveal pure eloquence. Though we share the same heart across three thousand *li*, I see your countenance clearly before me.

Having received your letter and opened it to read, I face the sealed envelope with tears falling like sleet. Your secluded dwelling is without cause; you have fabricated a false account of your origins.
Every word and every phrase is filled with sorrow; tears fall like a string of pearls. From afar, I call out to you at your thatched hut; the seasons have each reached their end.

Bind the mind to focus on a single object; at the crossroads, distinguish between the mundane and the transcendental. I address all my fellow practitioners: cultivate with diligence and do not be remiss.

Whether it be the words of the Buddha or the words of Pāpīyas, one must decisively discern between them. When asking for the way, seek the broad main road; advance with vigor as thunder rolls repeatedly.

This youth is indeed weak and submissive; my attachment to the tail of the steed is truly lingering. This mind, throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, strives with diligence, yet awaits but a fleeting flash of lightning.
Wielding the brush amidst ultimate sorrow, I am like a spring silkworm weaving its own cocoon. I repent, and again I repent; having taken this medicine, I suddenly feel dazed and nauseated.
One day, the needle shall come; together we shall carve the arrows for the lotus-drip water-clock. Though the lame tortoise may linger long, I shall not cease my vow for even an inch.
With a profound heart, I delight in the remaining radiance; with upturned heads, I look toward the leaders among the worthy. *Namo Amitābha*. Great Compassion spreads forth skillful means.
A Spontaneous Composition by Hezhigui (with Preface). Preface by Wang Jin:

Master Zhiguī invited me to compose verses in response to his own self-description. If I were to follow suit in every instance, I fear it would merely increase his attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Yet, if I were not to follow suit in every instance, I am already so eager that I find myself reluctant to stop.
I cannot. As for the poetic reflections on the grace of the Dharma, I have composed these verses in sequence:

Someone dreams of being a Confucian scholar; his stern demeanor is as brisk as the wind of his whip. He gazes into a mirror and adjusts his robes and cap; like a mountain pheasant, he preens his feathers and wings.

Looking back at the people of this world, footprints fill the melon fields. When one awakens from the dream in a single morning, one laughs until Li Taibai falls over (Taibai had a poem mocking Confucian scholars).

There was a man who dreamed he had become an immortal. Vast clouds billowed beneath his feet; riding upon the vital breath, he returned in an instant after having already traveled throughout the Three Isles.
Looking back at the people of the world, he saw how they wither prematurely in their youth. Yet when he awoke from the dream, his own body was ultimately no less subject to old age.
There is one who dreams of becoming a Buddha; through clarity, he establishes illumination. With a single mind, he returns to the Pure Land and grasps the secret essentials at the Zen gate.
Looking back at the people of the world, they measure one another with the narrow apertures of earthworms. When the dream is suddenly awakened, such deluded thoughts are truly laughable.
I am but an ordinary person; my body is constantly attached to rice porridge and cooked food. Whenever there is porridge or rice to eat, I stretch out my legs and sleep until dawn.
When asked about Confucianism, I do not know it; when asked about Chan, I do not realize it; when asked about the Way, I cannot grasp it. Dream upon dream, one transmits to another.
I, too, have wandered among the Confucians. Kongzi and Mengzi shine brightly upon the tablets and records; Cheng, Zhu, Lu, and Wang are like great Pengs spreading their twin wings.

How futile are those who, in their confusion, seek the sword—exhausting themselves in the traces of marking the boat! Only the spirit of loyalty and filial piety remains, as pure as ten thousand years of white iron-blossoms.
I, too, roam among the immortals; these various transcendents are vast and boundless. I constantly fear that the back of the giant turtle might overturn, submerging the islands within the sea.
Worldly men laugh at the lofty perfected ones, asking who among them will first wither away. Only those with loyalty and filial piety shall outlast heaven itself and never grow old.
I, too, roam within Chan; there is neither cessation nor illumination. I ask you, why is this so? Is it the essential or the non-essential of the Chan gate?
The old masters Zhaozhou and Yunmen—these two have not a single aperture. Only their loyal and filial hearts remain, causing patriarch after patriarch to break into a smile.
My friend knows where to return; elder brother, you shall be reunited with your mother. How noisy is this defiled land! How tranquil is that pure land!
Offering my liver to Amitābha, I spread my hair as a mat for him. Great indeed is the spirit of loyalty and filial piety; the three teachings mutually inform one another.
Concluding Colophon to the *Erlin Changhe Shi* (Poems of Mutual Response between the Two Forests) by Luo Gaoyao.
In the forty-first year of the Qianlong era, a gentleman from Zhejiang passed through Suzhou. His old friend, Mr.
Peng, presented this volume to me and requested that I correct those characters that deviated most significantly from antiquity.

Having read it once or twice, its mournful resonance rang out with crystalline clarity—like the plaintive yet harmonious cry of the kalaviṅka bird throughout the six periods of the day; it was as fragrant as the music of Mañjuśrī.
The *sā* flower is a fresh and beautiful petal. I think to myself that it has now been six years since I last composed a poem;
yet I remain foolishly deluded, wandering and adrift among men. My pure karma has been washed away until not even a speck remains, while my transgressions and afflictions are as vast as Mount Sumeru.
